questions.question: Define stability, strength and rigidity, and use a plastic ruler and a dry biscuit to show that strength and rigidity are different.
questions.expected_answer: Stability is the ability of a structure to stay upright and in position without toppling or sliding, depending on base, centre of gravity and anchoring. Strength is the ability of a material or structure to carry a load without breaking. Rigidity or stiffness is the ability to carry a load without bending or changing shape. A plastic ruler cannot be broken by pressing on its ends, so it is strong, but it bends easily, so it is not rigid; a dry biscuit holds its shape under a small load, so it is rigid, but snaps at once, so it is not strong.

questions.question: Describe the tubing investigation, state the result and explain it.
questions.expected_answer: A flat A4 sheet laid across a gap between two books sags under its own weight and collapses under a single coin. An identical sheet rolled into a tube about 3 centimetres across and taped, laid across the same gap, carries dozens of coins in a cup and stood on end holds a textbook, failing eventually by its wall buckling inward at the middle. A wider tube is stiffer but its thin wall buckles more easily, so there is an optimum diameter. The paper has not become stronger; in the tube the material is spread away from the centre, so bending requires the top of the wall to shorten and the bottom to stretch, which paper resists, making the tube rigid.

questions.question: Describe the folding investigation, including the effects of fold size and direction, and give three examples of folding used to stiffen materials.
questions.expected_answer: An A4 sheet folded along its length into sharp zigzag pleats about 2 centimetres wide and laid across the gap carries far more than the flat sheet, roughly as much as the tube, until a fold flattens. Narrow sharp folds are stiffer than wide shallow ones. A folded sheet laid with its folds parallel to the supports collapses at once, because the folds add no thickness in the direction of bending; folds must run along the span. Examples: corrugated iron roofing, the fluted core of corrugated cardboard, ribs pressed into car floor pans and tin lids, folded-plate concrete roofs, a paper fan, a palm leaf.
